title: Alkali Metals — General Characteristics
notes: **Group 1 elements:** Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na), Potassium (K), Rubidium (Rb), Caesium (Cs), Francium (Fr). All have the general electronic configuration ns¹ in their valence shell, giving them one loosely bound electron that is readily lost to form M⁺ ions. They are the most electropositive elements in each period and are never found free in nature due to their extreme reactivity with air and moisture.

**Physical properties — atomic and ionic radii:** Atomic radii increase down the group: Li (152 pm) < Na (186 pm) < K (231 pm) < Rb (244 pm) < Cs (262 pm). The increase is due to adding new electron shells. Ionic radii follow the same trend: Li⁺ (76 pm) < Na⁺ (102 pm) < K⁺ (138 pm) < Rb⁺ (152 pm) < Cs⁺ (167 pm). The Li⁺ ion is the smallest cation in aqueous solution (high hydration energy compensates for its small crystal radius), making it effectively larger in solution than Na⁺.

**Physical properties — density anomaly:** Density generally increases down the group (Li: 0.534, Na: 0.971, K: 0.862, Rb: 1.532, Cs: 1.93 g/cm³), but potassium is LESS dense than sodium (0.862 < 0.971). This anomaly occurs because the increase in atomic volume from Na to K is proportionally greater than the increase in atomic mass, due to the addition of a new electron shell (3p to 4s). All alkali metals are light enough to float on water, though they react violently with it.

**Physical properties — melting and boiling points:** Both decrease down the group: Li (181°C) > Na (98°C) > K (63°C) > Rb (39°C) > Cs (28°C). This is because metallic bond strength decreases as atomic size increases — the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and more delocalized, weakening the attraction between the cation and the electron sea. Li has the strongest metallic bond due to its small size, while Cs has the weakest. Mercury (bp 357°C) has a higher boiling point than caesium (bp 671°C) — wait, Cs bp = 671°C > Hg bp = 357°C. Cs has the lowest mp but relatively high bp due to its large atomic size.

**Flame test colours:** Alkali metals impart characteristic colours to flames due to excitation of the valence electron to higher energy levels, followed by emission when it returns to the ground state: Li — crimson red (λ = 670.8 nm), Na — intense golden yellow (λ = 589.0, 589.6 nm, the D-lines), K — lilac/pale violet (λ = 766.5, 769.9 nm), Rb — red-violet (λ = 780.0 nm), Cs — blue (λ = 455.5 nm). The colours are used in qualitative analysis and in pyrotechnics (Li for red, Na for yellow, K for blue-violet).

**Ionization enthalpy trend:** The first ionization enthalpy decreases down the group: Li (520 kJ/mol) > Na (496) > K (419) > Rb (403) > Cs (376). This reflects increasing atomic size and shielding — the valence electron is progressively farther from the nucleus and easier to remove. Despite Li having the highest IE, it is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution (see below) due to its extremely high hydration energy (−515 kJ/mol vs. Na⁺: −406, K⁺: −322 kJ/mol).

**Reducing power:** All alkali metals are strong reducing agents (they readily lose their valence electron). The standard reduction potential E°(M⁺/M) becomes less negative down the group: Li (−3.04 V) < Na (−2.71 V) < K (−2.93 V) < Rb (−2.98 V) < Cs (−2.92 V). Li is the STRONGEST reducing agent in aqueous solution despite having the highest ionization energy, because its small Li⁺ ion has the largest hydration energy, making the overall process (sublimation + ionization + hydration) most favorable thermodynamically.

**Chemical reactivity — with water:** All alkali metals react vigorously with water to produce the hydroxide and hydrogen gas: 2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g). The violence increases down the group: Li reacts steadily, Na melts and darts across the surface, K ignites the H₂ immediately, Rb and Cs explode on contact. The reaction is exothermic (ΔH < 0); the heat generated increases down the group because the metal's melting point decreases, allowing faster contact with water.

**Chemical reactivity — with oxygen:** Lithium forms the oxide (Li₂O), sodium forms the peroxide (Na₂O₂), and potassium, rubidium, and caesium form superoxides (MO₂). This trend reflects the decreasing lattice energy with increasing cation size — large cations (K⁺, Rb⁺, Cs⁺) stabilize the large superoxide anion (O₂⁻) better than small cations (Li⁺ stabilizes the small O²⁻). Reactions: 4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O; 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂; K + O₂ → KO₂. The peroxide and superoxide are paramagnetic due to unpaired electrons.

**Chemical reactivity — with hydrogen:** All alkali metals react with hydrogen at elevated temperatures to form ionic hydrides: 2M + H₂ → 2MH. These are saline (ionic) hydrides containing H⁻ ions. They are strong reducing agents and react violently with water: MH + H₂O → MOH + H₂. LiH is the most thermally stable (decomposes at ~850°C), while CsH is the least stable (decomposes at ~400°C), following the trend of decreasing lattice energy with increasing cation size.

**Diagonal relationship — Li and Mg:** Lithium shows remarkable similarity to magnesium (diagonal to it in the periodic table) due to similar charge densities (Li⁺: 5.6, Mg²⁺: 6.7) and polarizing power. Both form nitrides directly with N₂ (Li₃N, Mg₃N₂), both carbonates decompose on heating (Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂; MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂), both fluorides and phosphates are sparingly soluble, both form nitrides that hydrolyze to NH₃, and both form organolithium/Grignard reagents with similar reactivity. This is the only significant diagonal relationship in Group 1.

**Chemical reactivity — with halogens:** All alkali metals react vigorously with halogens to form ionic halides (MX): 2M + X₂ → 2MX. These are white, crystalline, high-melting solids soluble in water. LiF is the least soluble alkali halide (Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻³) due to its high lattice energy (small F⁻ and small Li⁺). CsI is the most soluble due to its lower lattice energy. All alkali halides are important industrial chemicals and occur naturally as minerals (e.g., halite NaCl, sylvite KCl).

**Diamagnetism of compounds:** All alkali metal compounds are diamagnetic because the M⁺ ion has a noble gas configuration (no unpaired electrons). Li⁺: 1s², Na⁺: [Ne], K⁺: [Ar], Rb⁺: [Kr], Cs⁺: [Xe]. The only paramagnetic alkali species is the neutral atom (ns¹) or the superoxide anion (O₂⁻ in KO₂). This makes alkali metal chemistry relatively simple magnetically compared to transition metals.

**Storage and handling:** Alkali metals must be stored under oil (kerosene, mineral oil) or in inert atmosphere (argon) to prevent reaction with atmospheric oxygen and moisture. Lithium is an exception — it is less dense than kerosene (0.534 g/cm³ vs. kerosene ~0.8 g/cm³) and floats, so it is stored in petrol or paraffin wax. Sodium is commonly stored in kerosene. Francium (radioactive, half-life 22 minutes) has never been collected in visible quantities and is studied only by tracer methods.

**Biological importance:** Na⁺ and K⁺ are essential electrolytes in biological systems. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump maintains a 10:1 intracellular K⁺ to extracellular Na⁺ ratio, which is critical for nerve impulse transmission, muscle contraction, and osmotic balance. Li⁺ salts (lithium carbonate, Li₂CO₃) are used as mood stabilizers in treating bipolar disorder. Rb and Cs have no known biological role and are potentially toxic.
confusion: Li is the strongest reducing agent despite highest ionization energy: Students expect the element with the lowest ionization energy (Cs) to be the strongest reducing agent. However, in AQUEOUS solution, Li has the most negative E° (−3.04 V) because the extremely high hydration energy of the tiny Li⁺ ion (−515 kJ/mol) more than compensates for its high ionization energy (520 kJ/mol). In the gas phase, Cs is indeed easier to oxidize, but aqueous chemistry involves solvation effects.

Diagonal relationship is Li-Mg, not Na-Ca: The diagonal relationship in Group 1 is between Li (period 2) and Mg (period 3, Group 2), not between Na and Ca. This is because Li⁺ and Mg²⁺ have similar ionic radii (76 vs. 72 pm) and similar charge densities, leading to comparable polarizing power and chemical behavior. Na⁺ (102 pm) does not have a diagonal match with similar properties.

Superoxides vs. peroxides — size matters: The type of oxide formed depends on the cation size. Small Li⁺ stabilizes O²⁻ (oxide, Li₂O); medium Na⁺ stabilizes O₂²⁻ (peroxide, Na₂O₂); large K⁺, Rb⁺, Cs⁺ stabilize O₂⁻ (superoxide, MO₂). The large superoxide anion (O₂⁻, radius ~180 pm) can only be stabilized by a large cation through favorable lattice energy. This is a classic example of Fajan's rules applied to oxide stability.

Flame test for Na vs. K — the yellow masks violet: Sodium's yellow D-line emission (589 nm) is extremely intense and can mask the weaker violet emission of potassium (766 nm). To observe potassium's flame colour in the presence of sodium contamination, view the flame through cobalt blue glass, which absorbs the yellow light but transmits violet. This is a standard technique in qualitative analysis.

All alkali compounds are colorless and diamagnetic: Alkali metal compounds contain M⁺ ions with noble gas configurations (no unpaired electrons) and anions that are also typically diamagnetic (O²⁻, Cl⁻, OH⁻). The only exception is the superoxide KO₂, which contains the paramagnetic O₂⁻ anion and is yellow-orange in color. All other alkali metal compounds are white/colorless and diamagnetic.
practice: Arrange the following in order of increasing reducing power in aqueous solution: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs. Explain why the order does NOT follow the ionization energy trend. Calculate the total energy change for Li(s) → Li⁺(aq) using: ΔH_sub(Li) = 161 kJ/mol, IE₁(Li) = 520 kJ/mol, ΔH_hyd(Li⁺) = −515 kJ/mol. Compare with Na: ΔH_sub = 108, IE₁ = 496, ΔH_hyd = −406 kJ/mol.

Explain why Li forms Li₂O (oxide) while K forms KO₂ (superoxide) when burned in air. Calculate the lattice energies using the Kapustinskii equation for Li₂O and KO₂ and explain the size-match principle. Why does Na form Na₂O₂ (peroxide) as the major product rather than oxide or superoxide?

A sample of commercial sodium contains 0.5% lithium as an impurity. Describe how you would: (1) detect the lithium impurity using flame test (explain the masking problem with sodium), (2) separate the lithium from sodium using fractional crystallization of their chlorides (solubility: LiCl 84 g/100g H₂O at 20°C, NaCl 36 g/100g H₂O at 20°C), (3) confirm the separation by atomic absorption spectroscopy.

Calculate the standard cell potential for the Li/Li⁺ (E° = −3.04 V) and K/K⁺ (E° = −2.93 V) couple. If a galvanic cell is constructed with Li anode and K cathode, what is E°cell? Explain why this cell would not work practically, considering the reactivity of both metals with water. What electrolyte would be required?

The diagonal relationship between Li and Mg explains several anomalies. Explain why: (1) Li₂CO₃ decomposes on heating while Na₂CO₃ does not, (2) LiF is sparingly soluble while NaF is soluble, (3) LiCl is soluble in ethanol while NaCl is not, (4) LiNO₃ decomposes to Li₂O + NO₂ + O₂ while NaNO₃ decomposes to NaNO₂ + O₂. Use the concept of polarizing power (charge/radius ratio) in your explanations.
universalFacts: Lithium is the lightest element and the lightest metal (density 0.534 g/cm³ — less than half that of water). It is so light that it floats on kerosene, which is why it must be stored under petrol or in paraffin wax. Lithium is also the only alkali metal that is solid at temperatures where all other alkali metals are liquid (mp 181°C vs. Na 98°C, K 63°C).

The sodium D-line (589.0 and 589.6 nm) is one of the most famous spectral lines in physics. It was discovered by Joseph von Fraunhofer in 1814 and was the first spectral line identified as arising from a specific element (Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen, 1859). The proximity of the two lines (spin-orbit coupling) was key evidence for the existence of electron spin.

Potassium is essential for human life — the average adult contains about 140 g of potassium, mostly as K⁺ ions. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump consumes approximately 20–40% of the body's resting energy to maintain the electrochemical gradient across cell membranes. Without this pump, nerve impulses could not propagate and muscles could not contract.

Francium is the rarest naturally occurring element — only ~20–30 grams exist in the entire Earth's crust at any given time, produced by the decay of actinium. Its most stable isotope (²²³Fr) has a half-life of only 22 minutes. Despite being the most electropositive element, no bulk chemistry of francium has ever been performed due to its extreme rarity and radioactivity.

The flame colours of alkali metals are used in pyrotechnics worldwide: lithium compounds (lithium carbonate, lithium chloride) produce red fireworks, sodium compounds (sodium nitrate) produce yellow, potassium compounds (potassium nitrate, potassium perchlorate) produce violet, and caesium compounds produce blue. The purity of these colours depends on avoiding sodium contamination, which would mask all other colours with its intense yellow emission.
